title: Collection expressions, immutable and frozen collections
body: Collection expressions (C# 12) create collections with one syntax for many target types: `int[] a = [1, 2];`, `List<int> l = [1, 2];`, `Span<int> s = [1, 2];`, `ImmutableArray<int> im = [1, 2];`. The spread element `..other` inlines another sequence: `[0, ..a, 9]`. The target type decides what is built, so the same expression can produce an array or a list.

Immutable collections (`System.Collections.Immutable`) never change after creation; operations such as `Add` return a new collection that shares structure with the old one. They are safe to share between threads and to hand out from APIs without defensive copies. Use builders (`ImmutableList.CreateBuilder<T>()`) when producing many items.

Frozen collections (`FrozenDictionary`, `FrozenSet`, .NET 8+) are read-only and optimized for lookup speed at the cost of slower creation. Create them once with `ToFrozenDictionary()` for configuration or lookup tables read many times.

Read-only interfaces (`IReadOnlyList<T>`, `IReadOnlyDictionary<K,V>`) describe what a caller may do, not whether the data can change; the producer may still mutate the underlying list. Immutable and frozen types guarantee the data cannot change.

Choose by the guarantee you need: a read-only view for encapsulation, an immutable collection for safe sharing with occasional updates, a frozen collection for build-once/read-many lookup. Check that 'immutable' items do not themselves contain mutable objects.
challenge: Build an ImmutableDictionary<string,int> of three stock levels, then produce a second version with one level changed using SetItem, and print the item from both versions to show the original is unchanged.
question: What does ImmutableList<T>.Add return?
correct: A new list containing the extra element; the original is unchanged
wrong: The same list instance with the element appended
reasoning: Immutable collections return new versions that share structure with the old one.
